title: Fake PayPal Suspension Notice
description: Read this email carefully. Click on anything that looks suspicious to flag it as a red flag.
subject: Your PayPal account has been suspended

redFlags.description: Fake sender domain — 'paypa1-security.com' uses the number '1' instead of the letter 'l'
Artificial urgency — '24 hours' deadline is designed to panic you into acting without thinking
Suspicious link — legitimate PayPal emails link to paypal.com, not third-party domains
Fake footer — '1 Fake Street, Scammer City' and 'PayPa1 Inc.' confirm this is fraudulent

bodyHtml:
PayPa1

Dear Valued Customer,

We have detected unusual activity on your account and have temporarily suspended your access for your protection.

To restore access, you must verify your identity within 24 hours or your account will be permanently closed.

Verify My Account Now

If you do not verify, we will be forced to permanently limit your account.

Thank you,
PayPal Security Team

© 2024 PayPa1 Inc. All rights reserved. | 1 Fake Street, Scammer City

title: IT Password Reset Scam
description: Your IT department appears to be asking you to reset your password. Spot the red flags.
subject: URGENT: Reset your password before 5PM today

redFlags.description: External domain — 'company-helpdesk.net' is not your company's official IT domain
Pressure deadline — forcing a same-day action is a manipulation tactic
Threatening language — 'locked out of all systems' is designed to create fear
Suspicious reset link — goes to an external domain, not your company's systems

bodyHtml:
🔒 IT Security Department

Dear Employee,

This is an URGENT notification requiring your immediate action today before 5:00 PM.

Failure to comply will result in your account being locked out of all company systems including email, VPN, and internal tools.

Please click the button below to reset your password:

Reset Password Now →

This link expires in 2 hours.

title: Prize Winner Scam
description: You've apparently won a prize. Find all the red flags in this email.
subject: 🎉 Congratulations! You've been selected as our winner!

redFlags.description: Fake domain — 'amazon-rewards-center.com' is not Amazon's official domain (amazon.com)
Unsolicited prize — you never entered this contest. Legitimate prizes require prior entry.
Advance fee fraud — asking for payment to claim a prize is always a scam
Credit card request — no legitimate prize requires your full card details

bodyHtml:
amazonrewards center

🎉🎊🏆

CONGRATULATIONS! You Are Our Lucky Winner!

Your email address was randomly selected from millions of Amazon users to receive a $1,000 Amazon Gift Card!

Please provide your credit card details below to complete your claim:

Card Number: ________________

CVV: _____ Expiry: ___/___

Offer expires in 24 hours. Act now!

title: CEO Business Email Compromise
description: This email appears to come from your CEO. Identify every red flag before taking action.
subject: Confidential - Urgent Wire Transfer Needed

redFlags.description: Lookalike domain — 'company-corp.co' mimics the real domain but uses .co instead of .com
Secrecy request — 'do not discuss with anyone' is designed to prevent you from verifying
Artificial urgency — 'within the next 2 hours' prevents careful verification
Unusual wire transfer request — executives never request wire transfers via email alone

bodyHtml:
From: Sarah Mitchell <smitchell@company-corp.co>

Hi,

I need you to process an urgent wire transfer today. I am currently in a board meeting and cannot be reached by phone.

Please do not discuss this with anyone else in the office as it is part of a confidential acquisition deal.

Please wire $24,500 USD to the following account:

Bank: First International Bank
Account Name: Meridian Consulting LLC
Account No: 4821937465
Routing No: 021000021

This needs to be completed within the next 2 hours. I will explain everything after the meeting.

Thanks for handling this quickly.
Sarah
Sarah Mitchell | Chief Executive Officer
company-corp.co | Direct: +1 (555) 847-2910

title: Microsoft Security Alert Spoof
description: A security alert from Microsoft. Examine the email carefully for signs of fraud.
subject: Action Required: Unusual sign-in activity on your Microsoft account

redFlags.description: Fake Microsoft domain — Microsoft emails come from @microsoft.com, not @microsoft-alerts.net
Fabricated location data — designed to create urgency and make the email seem personalized
Phishing link — hovering shows it goes to a non-Microsoft domain
Account suspension threat — used to create fear and rushed decision-making

bodyHtml:
Microsoft

Unusual sign-in activity

We detected something unusual about a recent sign-in to your Microsoft account.

Location: Lagos, Nigeria
Device: Unknown Windows Device
Time: Today at 3:42 AM

If you don't review this activity, your account may be suspended within 24 hours.

Review Recent Activity

Microsoft will never ask for your password in an email.

title: HR Benefits Enrollment Phish
description: An HR email about open enrollment. Identify what makes this email suspicious.
subject: ACTION REQUIRED: Complete your benefits enrollment by Friday

redFlags.description: External HR domain — your company's HR emails would come from your company's official domain
False deadline urgency — designed to prevent you from thinking carefully or verifying
SSN request — HR portals never ask for your full Social Security Number via email link
Suspicious portal link — goes to 'employee-portal-2024.com', not your company's official HR system

bodyHtml:
HR Benefits Portal

Dear Employee,

IMPORTANT: Open enrollment closes this Friday at 5PM. Employees who do not complete enrollment will be automatically removed from all benefit plans.

To complete your enrollment please log into our secure benefits portal:

Access Benefits Portal →

You will need your Employee ID and full Social Security Number to verify your identity and complete enrollment.

If you have questions contact hr-benefits@employee-portal-2024.com

title: Compromised Colleague Attack
description: An email from a real colleague. Look very carefully — something is wrong.
subject: Quick favor - can you review this before our meeting?

redFlags.description: Subdomain spoofing — 'docs.google.com.sharepoint-viewer.io' is owned by 'sharepoint-viewer.io', not Google
Credential request — legitimate shared documents don't ask for login credentials to view
Suspicious timing — unexpected document requests right before meetings are a common lure
No document preview — a real Google Doc link would show a recognizable preview, not a login page

bodyHtml:
Hey,

Just wanted to send this over before our 2pm. I made some updates to the Q4 budget doc — can you take a quick look and let me know if the numbers look right to you?

Here's the link:

https://docs.google.com.sharepoint-viewer.io/view?file=budget_Q4_final.xlsx

Note: You may need to sign in with your Google or Microsoft credentials to view the file.

[Document preview unavailable - click link to view]

Thanks!
James

title: Spear Phishing via LinkedIn Intel
description: A highly targeted email that uses your real professional details. Find every red flag.
subject: Re: Your talk at the Cybersecurity Summit last week

redFlags.description: Unverified publication domain — 'infosec-weekly.org' is not a recognized publication and cannot be verified
OSINT-based personalization — using public LinkedIn/conference data to appear legitimate is a spear phishing hallmark
Unsolicited attachment — a .docx file from an unverified sender can contain malicious macros
Macro enable request — asking to enable macros is a classic malware delivery technique

bodyHtml:
Hi,

I attended your presentation on zero-trust architecture at last week's Cybersecurity Summit and found your insights on lateral movement prevention particularly compelling.

I'm a staff writer at InfoSec Weekly and I'm working on a feature article about enterprise security leaders. I'd love to include some of your thoughts.

I've drafted a few interview questions in the attached document — would you be able to take a look?

📄

Interview_Questions_Final.docx

Note: Please enable macros when prompted to view formatted content

Looking forward to your response.

Best regards,
David Walsh
Staff Writer, InfoSec Weekly
infosec-weekly.org

title: Fake PayPal Login Page
description: This appears to be a PayPal login page. Click on everything suspicious.

redFlags.description: Fake domain — 'paypa1-secure-login.com' is not PayPal. The real site is paypal.com
No padlock/HTTPS indicator — a real payment site always has a valid SSL certificate shown in the browser
Password field on first page — PayPal separates login into two steps; combining them is a fake site pattern
Incorrect copyright — reads 'PayPa1' with the number 1 instead of the letter l

bodyHtml:
PayPal

title: Fake Microsoft 365 Login
description: A Microsoft 365 login page. Examine every detail carefully.

redFlags.description: Fake domain — 'microsoft365-auth.net' is not Microsoft. Real Microsoft login is login.microsoftonline.com
Slightly off logo — the Microsoft logo colors are subtly incorrect on fake sites
Pre-filled email — your email being pre-filled means the attacker already knows it and targeted you specifically
Missing legal links — fake sites often omit or have broken Terms of Use and Privacy links

title: Cloned Banking Portal
description: This bank login page looks very convincing. Find the subtle red flags.

redFlags.description: Subdomain spoofing — the real domain is 'account-verify.net', not 'firstnationalbank.com'. Read URLs right-to-left.
Wrong SSL certificate — the padlock is present but the certificate is issued to 'account-verify.net', not the bank
Excessive data collection — real bank logins never ask for your full debit card number on the login page
Broken help links — fake sites often have non-functional navigation links that go nowhere

bodyHtml:
🏦 First National Bank

Online Banking Login

🔒 account-verify.net [Certificate Details]
Help | Privacy Policy | Contact Us
